title: Service in the rule
hook: where and when you'll serve: young Nanak spent his trading money feeding hungry holy men and called it the true bargain
tomorrow: should you love a stranger's baby as much as your own nephew?

segments.voice: The stranger: Abraham promised a morsel and brought a feast. Today the welcome becomes a habit, with a day and a time.

Limited time. Best value. Don't miss this deal. Everyone is selling a good bargain. In the Sikh stories of Guru Nanak's youth, his father, Kalu, wanted one too. He gave his son money and sent him to market with a companion. Buy something, sell it for more, make a good bargain. Nanak came home with nothing. No goods, no money. And he told his father he'd made the truest bargain there is.
screen: `DON'T MISS THIS DEAL.` → `GO MAKE A GOOD BARGAIN.` → `HOME WITH NOTHING.` → `THE TRUEST BARGAIN?`

segments.voice: Here's what happened on the road, as Sikh tradition tells it. Nanak met a group of holy men who were hungry. Not a little hungry. They had nothing. So he spent all of it on food for them. His father was furious. That money was supposed to grow. But to Nanak, feeding the hungry was the real profit, the one that doesn't spoil. Sikhs call the story sacha sauda, the true deal. That's the puzzle solved: the bargain was true because of what it bought. And it seeds a Sikh teaching. Seva, selfless service, is woven into Sikh life, a duty and a joy at once. Sikh tradition links this story to langar, the free kitchen at the gurdwara, where anyone can come in, sit on the floor side by side, and eat the same meal. Volunteers cook, serve and wash up. Service, in this story, isn't a feeling. It's food, carried to hungry people, at an hour you can name. For a rule of life, that means writing down where and when you'll serve, so the deal actually gets made.
screen: `HUNGRY HOLY MEN ON THE ROAD.` · `SACHA SAUDA: THE TRUE DEAL.` · `SEVA: SELFLESS SERVICE.` · `LANGAR: ONE FLOOR, ONE MEAL.` · then, large: `SERVE.`

segments.voice: Name one place you could serve: a kitchen, a shelter, a neighbor, a friend's move. Picture your hands doing the work there: stirring a pot, folding a blanket, carrying one box. Then let your hands rest in your lap, and sit with the place you named.
Service in the rule: where and when you'll serve, written down, like Nanak's true bargain of food for the hungry.
Your line: serve. Nanak's father wanted a profit; Nanak bought a meal for the hungry. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1661 COUNTS.` → `OTHERS · 9 OF 10.` → `TOMORROW: SHOULD YOU LOVE A STRANGER'S BABY AS MUCH AS YOUR OWN NEPHEW?`

howItsDone: Sikhs practice seva, selfless service, and keep langar, the free community kitchen at the gurdwara, where volunteers cook and serve and everyone eats together on the floor. A rule of life can name a regular time and place to serve.

fork.setup: your friend has a bonus to spend and asks what Nanak's story would say. which fits the true bargain?

fork.reveal: Nanak didn't wait for the money to grow. He fed the hungry in front of him, and called that the true deal.
